zebralogic.title: Consolidate Direct Equivalences
zebralogic.principle: When a clue directly equates two attribute values, treat them as a single combined fact and propagate it to all related constraints.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue states that X is Y (e.g., "Peter has a bachelor's degree" or "the watermelon smoothie lover is Arnold").
zebralogic.example: Assigning Peter to a house but forgetting to also assign the bachelor's degree, treating the equivalence as unrelated.

zebralogic.title: Assign Fixed Positions Immediately
zebralogic.principle: If a clue fixes an attribute to a specific house number, place that attribute (and any directly linked attributes) in that house right away.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue says "Alice is in the third house" or any other positive placement.
zebralogic.example: Delaying placement of Alice in house 3 and later trying to infer it, leading to contradictory possibilities.

zebralogic.title: Translate 'N houses between' to Exact Distance
zebralogic.principle: Convert statements about a number of houses between two items into a precise positional distance (|pos(A) - pos(B)| = N+1).
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue says "There is one house between X and Y" or similar.
zebralogic.example: Treating "one house between" as adjacency and placing X and Y next to each other.

zebralogic.title: Enforce Adjacency for 'next to' and Ordered Left
zebralogic.principle: Translate adjacency clues ('next to', 'directly left of', 'directly right of') into exact positional constraints (pos(A) = pos(B) ± 1).
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue says "X is next to Y" or "X is directly left of Y".
zebralogic.example: Placing X two houses away from Y despite the clue saying they are next to each other.

zebralogic.title: Treat Consecutive Chains as a Block
zebralogic.principle: When multiple adjacency clues form a linear sequence, treat the whole chain as a block of consecutive houses in the given order to reduce permutations.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When you have two or more adjacency constraints that connect three or more items in a line.
zebralogic.example: Considering all permutations of A, B, C separately instead of recognizing they must occupy three consecutive houses in order.

zebralogic.title: Output Solution in Expected JSON Table Format
zebralogic.principle: Produce the final answer as a JSON object with a "header" array listing column names and a "rows" array of rows, matching the verifier's expected schema.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: After solving the puzzle, before returning the answer.
zebralogic.example: Returning a plain‑text table or a JSON with different keys, causing the verifier to reject the answer.

zebralogic.title: Keep Reasoning Concise to Avoid Token Truncation
zebralogic.principle: Limit the amount of explanatory text before the final JSON so the total output stays within the model's token limit.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When the reasoning is long and the answer must include the full solution.
zebralogic.example: Including a verbose step‑by‑step narrative that exceeds the token budget, causing the final JSON to be cut off.

zebralogic.title: Preserve Original Attribute Tokens (Case and Spelling)
zebralogic.principle: Copy attribute values verbatim from the problem statement, preserving exact case, spacing, and punctuation.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When writing the final solution, ensure each attribute value matches the original spelling.
zebralogic.example: Writing "German" instead of "german" or "Watermelon" instead of "watermelon", causing a mismatch.

zebralogic.title: Directional Ordering for 'somewhere to the left/right of' constraints
zebralogic.principle: Translate clues that state "X is somewhere to the left/right of Y" into a strict ordering constraint (pos(X) < pos(Y) or pos(X) > pos(Y)).
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue says "X is somewhere to the left of Y" without specifying adjacency.
zebralogic.example: Treating "X is somewhere to the left of Y" as adjacency and placing them next to each other.

zebralogic.title: Enforce Exclusion Constraints for Specific House Numbers
zebralogic.principle: When a clue states that an attribute cannot occupy a particular house, eliminate that house from the candidate set for that attribute.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue contains a negative placement (e.g., "X is not in house N").
zebralogic.example: Allowing the associate degree to be placed in house 2 despite a clue saying it is not.

zebralogic.description: Generating overly long reasoning before the final answer, causing token truncation.
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model tries to be thorough and does not account for the limited output length, leading to the solution being cut off.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Keep the reasoning concise and place the final JSON as early as possible; limit explanatory text to essential deductions.

zebralogic.description: Providing the solution in a format not recognized by the verifier.
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model is unaware of the exact JSON schema required by the evaluation script.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Always output a JSON object with "header" and "rows" keys exactly as specified.

zebralogic.description: Using incorrect case or synonyms for attribute values.
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model normalizes text or assumes case‑insensitivity, altering the original tokens.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Copy attribute tokens verbatim from the problem statement without changing case or spelling.

zebralogic.description: Misinterpreting adjacency constraints that involve a named entity and a non‑name attribute, treating them as non‑adjacent or placing both in the same house.
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model confuses adjacency with equality or overlooks that adjacency links two distinct houses across categories.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Remember that adjacency constraints always involve two different houses; they cannot be merged into one house.
